Good catch @SuperStrain — #27832 is definitely related! Both stem from the same root cause: OpenCode's built-in tools assume UTF-8 encoding. #27832 proposes broader multi-encoding support across Read/Grep/Edit/Write, while this issue specifically targets the ripgrep output parser crash when `lines.bytes` (base64) is returned instead of `lines.text`.

This issue's fix (handling the `bytes` variant in the Zod schema) would be a targeted first step that also benefits the broader #27832 effort. The parser should gracefully handle non-UTF-8 content even before full multi-encoding support lands.

Ran this branch locally against streaming markdown from a chat model and hit three correctness issues that don't show up in static-file tests. Filing them together since they share root causes (treating each container as "render-once" and missing concurrency guards).

### 1. Re-render is skipped after the first chunk (streaming use case)

`renderMermaidDiagrams` in `mermaid.ts` selects only containers without `data-mermaid-rendered`:

```ts
const containers = root.querySelectorAll(
  '[data-component="mermaid-diagram"]:not([data-mermaid-rendered])',
)
```

…and both `buildRenderedDOM` and `buildErrorDOM` set `data-mermaid-rendered="true"` on completion. That means once a container has been processed — even with a parse error — subsequent passes never look at it again.

**Repro:** the model streams a mermaid block in chunks. Chunk 1 arrives as `graph TD\n  A` (incomplete), `mermaid.render` throws, `buildErrorDOM` runs and locks the container. Chunk 2 completes the source to a valid `graph TD\n  A --> B`, but the container is now flagged and we keep showing the error bar forever. Same problem if chunk 1 is valid but chunk 2 changes the diagram structure — the new source is ignored.

**Suggested fix:** key the skip on source identity, not a boolean flag. Hash the source and store it on two attributes:

```ts
const MERMAID_SOURCE_ATTR = "data-mermaid-source-hash"
const MERMAID_LAST_GOOD_HASH = "data-mermaid-last-good-hash"

// Skip if last successful render matches current source.
// Retry if only a failed attempt is recorded — source may now be complete.
if (container.getAttribute(MERMAID_LAST_GOOD_HASH) === sourceHash) continue
if (container.getAttribute(MERMAID_SOURCE_ATTR) === sourceHash) continue
container.setAttribute(MERMAID_SOURCE_ATTR, sourceHash)  // mark attempt
// ...render...
container.setAttribute(MERMAID_LAST_GOOD_HASH, sourceHash)  // mark success
```

On failure, the existing rendered DOM (from the previous good chunk) stays visible while the model keeps streaming.

### 2. `mermaid.render` races between concurrent `<Markdown>` instances

`renderMermaidDiagrams` is awaited per-container inside a single call, but nothing prevents two `<Markdown>` components from calling it simultaneously. Mermaid v11 uses a shared offscreen container for layout measurement and is not concurrency-safe — concurrent renders produce orphan `<svg id="mermaid-...">` nodes in `document.body` and occasionally cross-pollinate output between blocks.

**Repro:** open a session that has mermaid blocks across multiple historical messages. Every `<Markdown>` mounts roughly simultaneously and each fires off `renderMermaidDiagrams(container)`. With 3+ blocks it reproduces reliably on Chrome.

**Suggested fix:** serialise every render through a module-level promise chain:

```ts
let mermaidRenderChain: Promise<unknown> = Promise.resolve()

export function renderMermaidDiagrams(root: HTMLElement): Promise<void> {
  const task = mermaidRenderChain.then(() => renderMermaidDiagramsImpl(root))
  mermaidRenderChain = task.catch(() => undefined)
  return task
}
```

Strictly sequential renders, fully backwards-compatible call signature.

### 3. Document-level click listeners leak per diagram

In `setupControlActions` (`mermaid.ts:552`):

```ts
document.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  if (downloadMenu.style.display === "none") return
  ...
})
```

This is attached every time a diagram is rendered and never removed. Each new mermaid block in a chat session adds another listener that stays alive for the lifetime of the page. The `container.addEventListener("click", ...)` a few lines above has the same issue. Re-mounting the `<Markdown>` (route change, search, etc.) compounds it.

**Suggested fix:** scope listeners per-render and clean them up. Either store an `AbortController` per container and trigger `.abort()` on re-render/unmount:

```ts
const ac = new AbortController()
container.addEventListener("click", ..., { signal: ac.signal })
document.addEvent

#23718 is the closest related issue, but this request is slightly broader. The main point here is not only that Cmder fails, but that old Windows environments without Windows Terminal support still rely on classic `conhost.exe` or conhost-based wrappers such as Cmder / ConEmu.

For those environments, users cannot always switch to Windows Terminal. So the request is for a safer TUI rendering fallback for old conhost-based terminals, rather than a fix for one specific Cmder regression.

#21277 and #26480 are also related Windows terminal issues, but they focus on crash cleanup / ConPTY exit behavior. This issue is specifically about rendering compatibility and fallback behavior for old Windows conhost environments.

**Additional finding: the tmux passthrough wrapper also has a double ESC byte bug**

I investigated the same issue with `tmux pipe-pane` hex dump capture and found an additional subtle code bug in the `writeOsc52()` function beyond the `allow-passthrough` discussion.

The template `\x1BPtmux;\x1B${osc52}\x1B\\` has an **extra `\x1B` (ESC) byte** between `tmux;` and `${osc52}`. Since `osc52` itself starts with `\x1B` (`ESC ]52;c;...`), the actual bytes sent are:

```
Expected: ESC P tmux; ESC ]52;c;base64 BEL ESC \
Actual:   ESC P tmux; ESC ESC ]52;c;base64 BEL ESC \
                          ^^
                     double ESC — NOTE the extra \x1B in the template:
                     `\x1BPtmux;\x1B${osc52}\x1B\\`
                                ^^  this ESC is the bug
```

Confirmed by tmux pane capture:

```
Offset  Hex                  ASCII
0518:   1b 50 74 6d 75 78 3b  ESC P t m u x ;
0525:   1b                     ← extra ESC byte  
0526:   1b 5d 35 32 3b 63 3b  ESC ] 5 2 ; c ; (OSC52 begins)
```

This extra ESC can cause the terminal to reject the OSC52 sequence.

The same template pattern appears in the GitHub source at:
**`packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/tui/util/clipboard.ts`**

**Fix**: Change `\x1BPtmux;\x1B${osc52}\x1B\\` to `\x1BPtmux;${osc52}\x1B\\` (remove the `\x1B` before the OSC52 payload).

**Workaround**: `env -u TMUX opencode` (unset `$TMUX` to skip the DCS wrapper entirely, letting tmux `set-clipboard on` handle raw OSC52 forwarding).

The TUI already supports word deletion and line clearing shortcuts out of the box:

1. Default bindings, the full content is here [Opencode TUI keybinds](https://opencode.ai/docs/zh-cn/keybinds/)

- input_clear — ctrl+c, clear all input, single line or multiple lines
- input_delete_to_line_start — ctrl+u, delete from cursor back to start of the line

2. You could also customize keybinds in ~/.config/opencode/tui.json, 'super' means 'CMD' key

```
{
  "keybinds": {
    "input_clear": "ctrl+c, super+delete"
  }
}
```

3. With tui.json configured, but CMD+Delete/Option+Delete still does not work in Opencode TUI, you could configure your terminal:

e.g. in iTerm2: Settings → Profiles → Keys → Add CMD+Delete → Send Escape Hex Codes 0x15 .    (this will make CMD+Delete same as CTRL+U, which is to delete to line start)

Current `dev` now accepts `directory` through `WorkspaceRoutingQueryFields`, and `WorkspaceRoutingMiddleware` uses `?directory=...` / `x-opencode-directory` to provide `WorkspaceRouteContext`; `InstanceContextMiddleware` then loads the instance context from that routed directory before `Session.create` runs.

Relevant current files:
- `packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/groups/session.ts` — `session.create` declares `query: WorkspaceRoutingQuery`
- `packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/workspace-routing.ts` — `defaultDirectory()` reads `directory` query/header and provides `WorkspaceRouteContext`
- `packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/instance-context.ts` — loads `InstanceStore` with `route.directory`

So the original behavior this PR targeted appears covered by the newer routing architecture. If anything remains useful here, it would be a fresh small test-only PR proving `POST /session?directory=...` persists the routed directory, rather than reopening this stale implementation branch.

@simonklee I dug deeper into the TUI plugin API as you suggested — here's what I found.
Short version: TUI plugins can't modify the permission prompt either.
Why — the full picture
I traced every potential path in TuiPluginApi (api.tsx (https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/dev/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/tui/plugin/api.tsx)):
- api.state — read-only snapshot of session/permission data
- api.ui.dialog — replace/setSize work, but PermissionPrompt is not a dialog, it's an inline component in the session layout
- api.slots.register — no slots in PermissionPrompt
- api.event.on — read-only events
- api.renderer — no component tree traversal API
- api.command/api.kv/api.theme — irrelevant

The root cause is in permission.tsx 
https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/ee16f08ffa35d564cf9a7149a69c43e8a6817b3f/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/tui/routes/session/permission.tsx#L542
https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/ee16f08ffa35d564cf9a7149a69c43e8a6817b3f/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/tui/routes/session/permission.tsx#L645

```
const [store, setStore] = createStore({
    expanded: false,  // hardcoded: can't start expanded
});
// ...
maxHeight: 15,      // hardcoded: can't be taller
```

This is local Solid.js state inside a component. No plugin API — server or TUI — can reach into it.

## Real-world use case: toggle auto-review without LLM round-trip

I'm building [opencode-review](https://github.com/sun-praise/opencode-review), a plugin that runs automated code reviews when a session goes idle. It has a `/review:auto` slash command to toggle auto-review on/off.

**Current problem:** The command does literally one thing — flip a boolean — but it must spin up an LLM agent to do it. The flow is:

```
User types: /review:auto off
  → command.execute.before hook (can't cancel)
  → LLM agent receives a prompt: "if args contain 'off', call toggle_auto_review(enabled: false)"
  → LLM calls the toggle tool
  → Tool sets autoEnabled = false
```

This wastes tokens and adds ~1-2s latency for what should be an instant operation. It also feels fragile — the LLM might misunderstand the instruction or do something unexpected.

**What I need:** A way for the `command.execute.before` hook to:
1. Parse the argument (`on`/`off`)
2. Set the state directly
3. Return a response to the user
4. **Skip the LLM call entirely**

**Workaround I'm considering:** Use `command.execute.before` to do the actual toggle work, then replace `output.parts` with a simple instruction so the LLM just echoes the result. Still wastes a call but at least the logic is deterministic.

Would love to see the `noReply` / `cancelled` flag merged. Happy to help test if needed.
